newsitem.title: USA: US weighs more help for blizzard-stricken Dakotas.
newsitem.headline: US weighs more help for blizzard-stricken Dakotas.

text.p: Agriculture Department officials Monday were considering more emergency aid to blizzard-stricken ranchers in the Dakotas as forecasters said they did not see any break in the deadly, frigid conditions plaguing the upper Midwest.

Unofficial estimates were that as many as 50,000 head of cattle had perished in the prolonged Arctic conditions of the northern Great Plains and that this number could triple by the time the fierce winter storms are over.

North and South Dakota have suffered freezing temperatures and heavy snow since November, with barely a noticeable break. Snowfall has been more than double normal in many areas, with some regions blanketed by more than six feet since the fall.

Low temperatures and high winds have combined to produce life-threatening conditions. Wind chills this past weekend were measured as low as 50 below zero, and forecasters issued dire predictions of continued subzero temperatures, high winds generating even lower wind chills and possibly heavier snowfalls in February and March.

"There does not appear to be any break in sight for the region," Agriculture Department meteorologist Brad Rippey said. "And as you get closer to spring they tend to get heavier snowfalls. They have a long winter ahead of them yet."

Agriculture Department officials scheduled a meeting Monday to brief Secretary Dan Glickman on the situation and to discuss emergency measures to help ranchers get feed to their marrooned animals. "We're considering anything we can that we think might help," a department official said.

Responding to calls for more help from Senators Tom Daschle, Democrat of South Dakota, and Byron Dorgan, Republican of North Dakota, the department decided late Friday to give snow-bound ranchers more time to enroll in an emergency feed programme that will provide $1.4 million to producers to either buy feed for their cattle or lease equipment to clear roads to the trapped animals.

The department also lifted rules that make Dakota ranchers eligible to participate in a cost-share programme under which the government provides 30 percent of the money needed to buy extra feed and farmers come up with the rest.
Also under consideration is implementing a new emegency feed programme that would increase available funds beyond the $1.4 million already authorised.
